clue.text: Put in order: fish, one small fish, gutted

parts.note: the cod is a common food fish
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: a gutted fish has had its insides removed, so the middle of the word for small fish goes

parts.note: fry are young, newly hatched fish

explanation.surface: Someone sorting a fishmonger's slab: a fish, then a tiny gutted one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' strips the middle letter from FRY, leaving FY. 'Put in order' looks like a filing instruction and is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To codify is to arrange rules or laws into a systematic code, which is putting them in order.

clue.text: Offensive politician a soldier knocked over in the loo?

indicators.note: the politician, a and upturned soldier sit inside the word for the loo

parts.note: can is American slang for a toilet
MP, Member of Parliament

indicators.note: something knocked over is upended, so the soldier's letters are read backwards

parts.note: GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A political scandal: an MP has toppled a soldier inside a lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' reads as an adjective about the loo scene, but it is a military noun here; 'loo?' warns of the American slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A campaign is a military offensive, an organised attack sustained over time.

clue.text: Agreement to limit combat leads to discharge

indicators.note: the agreement's letters hem in the combat word, setting bounds round it

parts.note: a deal is an agreement
a fray is a fight or skirmish

explanation.surface: A ceasefire deal that curbs fighting results in troops being sent home.
explanation.definitionFit: Defrayal is the payment of costs, i.e. the discharge of an expense or debt.

clue.text: Light feminine sparkly material …

parts.note: F is the grammatical abbreviation for feminine
lamé is a fabric woven with metallic threads

explanation.surface: Describing a dress: light, feminine, made of glittering cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the surface on into 5 Down, but this clue stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A flame gives off light, so the word serves as a noun for a source of light.

clue.text: Put in order, keeping a model satisfied

indicators.note: the word for put in order holds a and the model inside it

parts.note: placed means arranged or set in position
the Model T was Ford's famous car

explanation.surface: Arranging things neatly while humouring a fashion model to keep her happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Placated means appeased or calmed, the state of being satisfied after a grievance.

clue.text: … unusually clean material for soldier

indicators.note: letters arranged unusually are put in an unexpected order

parts.note: corporal as an adjective means bodily or physical, i.e. material

explanation.surface: Continuing 3 Down: a strangely clean fabric for a soldier's uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' turns CLEAN into LANCE. 'material' looks like cloth again but is the adjective meaning physical.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance corporal is the lowest-ranking non-commissioned officer in the British Army.

clue.text: Revolution in Cuba reformed law there

parts.note: C is the international vehicle code for Cuba

indicators.note: a law reformed is remade, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A political revolution in Cuba has brought legal reform there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' rearranges LAW THERE into ARTWHEEL. 'Revolution' suggests politics but means a turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartwheel is a sideways gymnastic turn of the whole body, one full revolution.

clue.text: No German follows you in France to find a station

indicators.note: the German word is placed after the French one

parts.note: tu is the familiar French for you
nein is German for no

explanation.surface: A European language muddle while hunting for a railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: To tune in is to adjust a radio to pick up a particular broadcasting station.

clue.text: Fuel runs out before rival ends

parts.note: dies means comes to an end, peters out

indicators.note: the closing letters of the two words before and rival are taken

explanation.surface: A motor race: one car's fuel runs dry before its rival's does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' looks like a position word but supplies its last letter, E; 'rival' gives L.
explanation.definitionFit: Diesel is a heavy oil used as fuel in compression-ignition engines.

clue.text: Mob's intention to hold absolutely nothing back

definitions.note: read as 'Mob is', so the definition is the noun mob, the 's a link

indicators.note: the whole combination is read backwards
the intention word holds the nothing word inside it

parts.note: aim means intention or purpose
FA, short for sweet FA, is British slang for nothing at all

explanation.surface: A gangster's aim is to keep absolutely everything for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet FA' is British slang for nothing at all; 'back' reverses the whole container, not just one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mafia is the organised crime syndicate, often called the Mob in America.

clue.text: Learner on farm looking to the future

parts.note: L is the learner-driver plate
a grange is a country house with farm buildings

explanation.surface: A trainee on a farm thinks ahead to the coming seasons.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-range plans or forecasts cover a distant period, so they look well ahead.

clue.text: Possibly a kilolitre brew of liqueur is made

indicators.note: a brew is a mixture stirred together, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A huge batch of liqueur is being made, perhaps a thousand litres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks a kilolitre as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilolitre is a unit of volume for liquids, one example of such a unit.

clue.text: Classical position of president in square-dancing

indicators.note: the president sits inside the jumbled letters
letters dancing jig about into a new order

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, US president

explanation.surface: A president at a square dance strikes a classical pose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square-dancing' looks like a single folk-dance term; split it, and 'dancing' scrambles 'square' around Lincoln's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical ballet an arabesque is a pose on one leg with the other extended behind.

clue.text: Chicanery surrounding start of Hanoverian period

indicators.note: the trickery word goes round the letter taken

parts.note: a wile is a trick or piece of cunning

indicators.note: the opening letter of Hanoverian is taken

explanation.surface: Political trickery at the dawn of the Hanoverian era in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hanoverian period' reads as one phrase; split it, and 'period' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A while is an indefinite stretch of time, a period.

clue.text: Man used to going Dutch?

parts.note: 'Dutch' is old cockney slang for a wife (my old Dutch), so this is a man accustomed to his wife being away, not to splitting a bill

explanation.surface: A man who habitually splits the bill on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going Dutch' suggests sharing costs; read 'Dutch' as wife and 'going' as leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: A man whose wife is often away for long periods is called this, the male form of the term.

clue.text: During function, Liberal joins right-wing plot

indicators.note: the joined pieces come in the middle of the function word

parts.note: sine is a trigonometric function

indicators.note: the Liberal letter is attached after the right-wing word

parts.note: a Tory is a British Conservative

explanation.surface: At a political function, a Liberal teams up with a right-wing conspiracy.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyline is the plot of a novel, film or play.

clue.text: Regularly sits up pining, burning the midnight oil

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals: first, third, fifth

parts.note: dying for something means pining or longing for it

explanation.surface: Someone sits up late at night, pining, unable to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Burning the midnight oil is the idiom for working, especially reading, late into the night.

clue.text: Not well up in prose?

definitions.meaning: ignorant of, inexperienced in a subject
prose is writing not set in verse, so whimsically it is not put into verse

explanation.surface: Someone unfamiliar with prose writing.
explanation.definitionFit: To be unversed in a subject is to lack knowledge of it; prose is literally writing without verse.

clue.text: Well-travelled commanders grouse about petty officer, drunk

parts.note: COs are commanding officers

indicators.note: the complaint word goes round the other pieces

parts.note: to grouse is to moan or complain
PO is a petty officer in the navy
lit is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Seasoned officers grumble about a drunken petty officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosmopolitan person has travelled widely and is at home in many countries.

clue.text: Strikes gain strength, it's said

indicators.note: the pronunciation of the word heard is what counts, not its spelling

parts.note: the moon waxes, growing larger and stronger

explanation.surface: Industrial strikes grow more powerful, so people report.
explanation.definitionFit: Whacks are hard blows, as in strikes with a stick or hand.

clue.text: Country's official staff arrested by troops

definitions.note: read as 'Country is', the 's a link

indicators.note: the gunners hold the staff, as if detaining it

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery
a wand is a rod of office carried by an official

explanation.surface: A nation's government employees are detained by the army.
explanation.definitionFit: Rwanda is a landlocked nation in east-central Africa.

clue.text: Welcome the way Derby's turned out

parts.note: how means the way or manner

indicators.note: a room turned out is emptied, so the innards of Derby go, leaving its outside letters

parts.note: the word Derby, with 's read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A greeting described by how race-day at Derby turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: Derby is an English city and also a famous horse race; 'turned out' empties it to DY.
explanation.definitionFit: Howdy is an informal American greeting, a word of welcome.

clue.text: Passage used by ground staff to publicise game?

parts.note: to air an opinion is to make it public
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: Airport workers using a corridor to promote a card game.
explanation.definitionFit: An air bridge is a movable enclosed walkway linking an airport gate to the aircraft door.

clue.text: Counter Murphy's raised, for example

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means read from the bottom up

parts.note: murphy is slang for a potato, which is a tuber; 's reads as 'is'

explanation.surface: Someone's raised a counter-argument, Murphy for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for example' signals that a murphy (potato) is one example of a tuber.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebut is to counter an argument or charge with evidence.

clue.text: Recurrent investment of new group from the East in traditional fuel

indicators.note: investment here means enclosing, as a besieging army invests a town

parts.note: coal is the traditional fuel for hearths

indicators.note: in an across clue, read from the east is right to left

parts.note: a unit is a group, as in a military unit

explanation.surface: A recurring Asian group investing in old-fashioned fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'investment' is the siege sense, surrounding; 'from the East' in an across clue means read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Continual means happening again and again, recurring frequently.

clue.text: Puts up money to release sporting accessories

definitions.meaning: pays a sum to free someone from custody until trial
in cricket, the two small crosspieces resting on top of the stumps

explanation.surface: Someone pays to free a person and get back their sports kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket's two wooden crosspieces atop the stumps share a name with paying for a prisoner's release.

clue.text: Small bowlers for long-haul travellers?

parts.note: pacemen are fast bowlers in cricket

explanation.surface: Short cricket bowlers going on a long journey.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, pacemen bowl fast; the question mark marks the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronauts travel immense distances into space, a jokey stretch of long-haul.

clue.text: Displayed last of art framed by retired artist

indicators.note: the painter's reversed name surrounds the letter like a frame
retired means withdrawn, so the painter's name runs backwards

parts.note: Edgar Degas, French Impressionist painter

indicators.note: the final letter of art is taken

explanation.surface: A gallery shows the last work of an artist who has stopped painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns DEGAS into SAGED, which holds T.
explanation.definitionFit: Staged means put on show, presented to an audience, as in exhibited.
